title: CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) over TCP, TLS, and WebSockets
summary: CoAP was designed to run over UDP, but some environments do better with reliable transports. This document defines how to carry CoAP over TCP, TLS and WebSockets, including changes to the message format and how connections are managed.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8323 carries CoAP requests and responses over TCP, TLS and WebSockets. The reliable transport handles delivery, while CoAP uses new message framing and signaling to manage each connection.

questions: how does coap framing work over tcp
what is a coap csm message
subtitle: How CoAP uses TCP, TLS and WebSockets when UDP is unavailable or unsuitable.

tldr.problem: CoAP was designed for UDP, but some networks block UDP, and browser applications may have access only to WebSockets.
tldr.mechanism: CoAP over reliable transports uses a length-prefixed frame instead of the UDP message header's type and message ID. Connection signaling exchanges capabilities, checks health and closes or aborts connections.
tldr.outcome: The specification defines CoAP over TCP, TLS and WebSockets, plus BERT block-wise transfers and four URI schemes. It updates RFC 7641 and RFC 7959 and is updated by RFC 8974.

today: RFC 8323 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7641 and RFC 7959, and is updated by RFC 8974. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why CoAP Uses Reliable Transports
sections.content:
The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) was designed for constrained devices using UDP. Some networks block or restrict UDP, while TCP and TLS may be available. TCP also provides congestion and flow control, and WebSockets can carry CoAP for applications running in a web browser.

The RFC still recommends CoAP over UDP, including DTLS over UDP, for constrained networks. CoAP over TCP can require more code, memory, packet space and connection round trips, so it is intended for situations where the network leaves no other choice. This document also adapts resource observation and block-wise transfer for reliable connections.
sections.plainLanguage: CoAP normally uses UDP, but some networks do not carry UDP traffic. This RFC lets CoAP use reliable transports in those cases, with additional resource costs.

sections.title: Framing CoAP Messages over a Byte Stream
sections.content:
UDP datagrams keep CoAP messages separate and provide their length. A TCP byte stream does not, so CoAP over TCP adds a length field. TCP already retransmits data and delivers it in order, so CoAP removes the Type and Message ID fields used for UDP reliability and duplicate detection. It also removes the Version field.

The first byte contains a 4-bit Len and a 4-bit token length. Len values 0 through 12 directly give the number of following option-and-payload bytes. Values 13, 14 and 15 signal an 8-bit, 16-bit or 32-bit extended length, with offsets defined by the RFC. The Code, Token, Options and optional Payload follow.
sections.plainLanguage: A byte stream needs a length marker so the receiver can find each message boundary. CoAP also removes its UDP-only reliability fields because TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery.

sections.title: Connection Setup and Signaling
sections.content:
Each endpoint must send a Capabilities and Settings Message (CSM) first on a new connection. It can advertise a maximum message size and support for block-wise transfer. A missing or invalid CSM is a connection error. Requests can be sent in either direction and asynchronously; Tokens distinguish concurrent requests, and each response returns on the same connection as its request.

Signaling messages include CSM, Ping, Pong, Release and Abort. A receiver must answer Ping with Pong using the same Token. Release asks the peer to close the connection in an orderly way; Abort means the sender cannot continue and closes immediately. Empty messages can act as basic keepalives. Application code decides when to open or reopen connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Both endpoints first announce their connection capabilities. Later signaling messages can test the connection, request an orderly close or report that communication must stop immediately.

sections.title: WebSockets, BERT and Resource Observation
sections.content:
CoAP over WebSockets uses binary WebSocket messages and the TCP framing format, except that Len is zero because the WebSocket frame already gives the length. The client includes the coap subprotocol in its opening handshake. The connection can carry several requests, and the transport provides reliable, ordered delivery.

Block-wise transfer remains useful for large messages and gateways. BERT is enabled by a Block1 or Block2 option with SZX value 7; it allows one message to carry multiple blocks of 1024 bytes. For observed resources, reliable delivery removes the need for notification sequence numbers and confirmable message types. A client cancels an observation with a GET request using the observation Token and Observe value 1; closing the connection removes its observations.
sections.plainLanguage: WebSockets carries CoAP messages in binary frames, with the WebSocket frame supplying their length. BERT lets a reliable-transport message carry several blocks, while an observation ends when the client deregisters or the connection closes.

sections.title: URI Schemes for Each Transport
sections.content:
The RFC defines four URI schemes: coap+tcp, coaps+tcp, coap+ws and coaps+ws. The first pair identifies CoAP over TCP, with TLS for the secure scheme. The second pair identifies CoAP over WebSockets, with TLS for coaps+ws. Resources under different schemes have distinct identities even when their authority is the same.

The default ports are 5683 for coap+tcp, 5684 for coaps+tcp, 80 for coap+ws and 443 for coaps+ws. WebSocket URIs use the well-known endpoint path /.well-known/coap; the remaining URI path and query identify the CoAP resource.
sections.plainLanguage: The URI scheme tells a client which transport to use and whether it must secure the connection. The path and query identify the CoAP resource at that endpoint.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
A security solution for CoAP over reliable transports must be implemented and enabled by default. The RFC defines a TLS binding and permits other suitable security layers. NoSec mode is optional to implement; a TLS mode using PreSharedKey, RawPublicKey or Certificate credentials is mandatory to implement, depending on the device's credential type.

For TLS over TCP, the RFC refers constrained devices to the TLS guidance in RFC 7925 and less-constrained deployments to RFC 7525. A client using coaps+ws must perform a TLS handshake. A peer must not assume that an alternative address offered in a signaling message inherits the security properties of the current connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations must include a security solution and enable it by default. If a peer suggests a different address, the client must check that connection's security separately.

items.desc: Answers Ping with the same Token.

items.desc: The sender cannot continue and closes the connection.
